name: RHA fillers (Teoxane)

lead: RHA fillers are Teoxane's hyaluronic acid gels, sold as Teosyal RHA outside the US and RHA Redensity in the US. They are designed to flex with facial expression, so people use them around the mouth and lips and in under-eye hollows for smoother lines and a filled look that moves naturally.

A cross-linked HA gel that keeps long HA chains adds soft volume and stretches with movement, then degrades gradually. A 52-week randomized study reported benefit for dynamic perioral lines, and trials have studied under-eye hollows, lips and nasolabial folds.

paras: A licensed clinician injects the area in an office visit and the filled look is visible immediately. People repeat treatments as the gel absorbs, and it can be dissolved with hyaluronidase.
Reported effects include swelling and bruising, and a case report describes hypersensitivity. It is a prescription medical device, results are temporary, and community discussion is thin.

chain: Flexible HA gel moves with face
angle.text: RHA fillers are designed to stay natural in areas that move, so people use them around the mouth and lips and in under-eye hollows. The flexible hyaluronic acid gel fills lines and hollows with a look that follows expression. Randomized perioral and under-eye trials support these uses.

lead: RHA (Resilient Hyaluronic Acid) fillers are cross-linked hyaluronic acid (HA) gels made by the Swiss company Teoxane, sold as Teosyal RHA outside the United States and as RHA Redensity in the US. They were developed for areas of the face that move with expression, such as the lines around the mouth, the lips and the under-eye region, where a gel has to stretch and recover as the face animates. [1][2]

People use them to soften wrinkles and folds, add lip fullness, fill hollows beneath the eyes and restore volume in the midface. Because HA attracts water, the gel adds volume as soon as it is placed, and the result is temporary: the body gradually breaks the gel down, so treatment is repeated over time. [3][4]

The range has been studied in randomized, evaluator-blinded trials for dynamic perioral lines, lips and nasolabial folds, and in registrations for infraorbital hollows. Teoxane has also published photonumeric scales for grading lip fullness, infraorbital hollows and midface volume that are used as trial endpoints. [1][5][6][7][8][9][10]
infobox: Gel that stretches with facial movement
Perioral lines, lips, nasolabial folds, infraorbital hollows, midface

paras: The RHA range uses a manufacturing process intended to keep long HA chains intact, so the gel is described as flexible and resilient in motion rather than stiff. [1] The collection is numbered RHA 1 to 4, with the lower numbers designed for finer areas and the higher numbers for deeper or more structural placement; RHA 3 has been approved in Europe for lip volumization. [2][5]

Like most HA fillers, the products are cross-linked so the gel lasts longer than uncross-linked HA, which is broken down quickly in tissue. Laboratory studies have compared how different cross-linking technologies change HA gel behavior [11] and how easily commercial cross-linked HA fillers can be injected with a standard method. [12] Technique articles describe midface volumization with gels designed for dynamic facial movement. [2]

Cosmetic uses include dynamic perioral lines (the vertical lines around the mouth), nasolabial folds, lip augmentation, infraorbital hollows (tear-trough area) and midface volume deficit. [1][5][6][7][2]

The manufacturer has also developed grading scales, the Teoxane Lip Fullness Scale and the Teoxane Infraorbital Hollows Scale, to describe how a treatment changes these areas in clinical practice and trials. [8][9]

HA is a sugar polymer found naturally in skin that binds water. In a filler it is chemically cross-linked into a gel, commonly with BDDE, which slows enzymatic breakdown and so lengthens the time it stays in the tissue. [4] The gel gives immediate volume, and most wrinkle fillers are temporary, with effects described as lasting around six months depending on product, area and individual. [4]

Practitioners choose gel firmness to match the area. Teoxane describes RHA gels as adapting to facial animation, an attribute assessed in the lip study through patient-rated natural look and feel. [2]

The FDA states that dermal fillers are regulated as medical devices that should be injected by licensed, trained providers. Its page lists bruising, redness, swelling, pain and itching as common effects, and rarer problems including infection, nodules, allergic reactions and accidental injection into a blood vessel, which can cause tissue damage or vision loss. [13]

A case report describes a hypersensitivity reaction to an RHA filler. [14] Late-onset swelling in the periocular area after HA filler has been reported in a six-patient case series treated with hyaluronidase and collagenase. [15] A study of multidose hyaluronidase examined breakdown of resilient HA fillers in vitro, relevant to how clinicians dissolve unwanted HA. [16]

In the EU and UK, fillers are non-prescription medical devices carrying a CE mark, which covers manufacturing standards rather than proof of efficacy; in the US they are approved by the FDA as devices. [4]

Hyaluronic acid was first isolated in 1934 by Karl Meyer and John Palmer from the vitreous body of a cow's eye; it is a long, unbranched sugar polymer that is a major component of skin, where it helps hold water and keep tissue open. [17] Injected as a gel, it absorbs water and swells to soften lines and restore volume, with effects that Wikipedia reports lasting roughly six to twelve months, and the FDA has approved the use. [17]

Native hyaluronic acid breaks down quickly in tissue, so most fillers are chemically cross-linked, commonly with BDDE (1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether), to make the gel more durable and resistant to enzymes. Cross-linking density affects stiffness, how fast the gel degrades, and how it behaves in different parts of the face. [4] Fillers can be placed with a sharp needle or a blunt micro-cannula. [17]

RHA stands for resilient hyaluronic acid and is the name of Teoxane's range of fillers. A 2022 randomised trial describes RHA Redensity as developed to optimise outcomes in highly mobile facial areas, and registered studies of RHA products cover perioral lines, nasolabial folds, lips and the infraorbital region. [1][5][6][7][18]

In the United States, dermal fillers are regulated as medical devices and must be injected by a licensed provider, with only a small number of fillers approved relative to the large number of CE-marked products on the European market; CE marking confirms manufacturing standards but does not itself require proof of efficacy. [4] The FDA maintains a consumer page listing approved fillers and their indications. [13]

Common reactions to hyaluronic acid fillers are bruising, redness, swelling, pain and itching. Less common problems include infection, lumps, delayed inflammatory reactions and allergic responses. [4] The most serious are vascular events, in which filler enters or compresses a blood vessel; Wikipedia notes embolisation into the eye's arteries can cause permanent vision loss and that delayed skin necrosis is also described. [4]

Hyaluronic acid fillers are distinctive in that the enzyme hyaluronidase breaks down hyaluronic acid, and clinical papers describe its use to dissolve filler for complications or unwanted results. [16][15][17] A case report describes a hypersensitivity reaction to an RHA filler, illustrating that reactions are documented for this brand as for others. [14]

People use hyaluronic acid fillers to soften lines around the mouth and nose, add lip volume, restore midface volume and reduce hollowing under the eyes, all areas that RHA studies have examined. Perioral lines are described as a highly mobile region where RHA was developed to perform well. [5][6][7] Results appear immediately, which differs from treatments that rely on gradual collagen change, and the effect is temporary, so fillers are re-treated over time. [17][4]

Perioral lines: a 52-week randomized, evaluator-blinded, no-treatment-controlled study evaluated RHA Redensity for moderate-to-severe dynamic perioral rhytides. [1] The related registration enrolled 202 participants. [5]

Lips: a randomized, double-blinded, multicenter US study of 202 patients tested RHA 3 against an active comparator, with the primary endpoint of noninferiority on the Teoxane Lip Fullness Scale at 12 weeks and secondary measures including satisfaction and natural look and feel to 52 weeks. RHA 3 met the noninferiority criterion. [7][8][19]

Nasolabial folds: registered trials compared Teosyal RHA gels with Juvederm Ultra XC (n=148) and Perlane-L (n=140). [20][3] A separate split-face randomized pilot funded by Teoxane compared a monophasic with a biphasic HA filler for nasolabial folds, finding comparable results with a trend favouring the monophasic gel. [21]

Under the eyes and elsewhere: a no-treatment-controlled infraorbital trial (n=248) is registered, and a trial in Chinese adults (n=260) is recruiting. [6][18] Routine-practice data include a prospective registry reporting one-year effectiveness and safety of HA fillers, a real-world periorbital study and a retrospective ultrasound study of skin density after an HA-based hydrogel. [22][23][24]

RHA is rarely discussed by name in forums. Filler discussions there generally concern lips, cheeks, chin and under-eye treatment with HA products as a group, with RHA appearing as one brand among many offered by clinics.
